strengths: Well-motivated physical framing: augmenting graph representations with a reciprocal-space (diffraction-inspired) branch to address the genuine limitation of finite-cutoff, local encoders failing to capture long-range periodic correlations.

Extensive experiments spanning three large benchmark suites (Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, MatBench) and many properties (formation energy, band gap, bulk/shear/Young's modulus, metal/non-metal classification, exfoliation energy, dielectric constant), with consistent improvements over a good set of recent strong baselines (Matformer, Crystalformer, Crystalframer, eComFormer, etc.).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (diffraction module, multi-head attention, residual connections, edge features) replicated across all three datasets, plus a targeted comparison between the learned pseudo-particle form factor and fixed tabulated X-ray form factors that directly supports the core design choice.

A formal invariance argument (Eqs. 18-19) showing the diffraction feature is invariant under crystallographic symmetry operations, complementing the standard E(3)-invariance argument for the graph branch.
Good reproducibility effort in the appendix: detailed hyperparameters for all baselines, a worked forward-propagation case study (CaF2), and explicit algorithm listing.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim -- that existing SOTA models (including already 'complete'/invariant models such as eComFormer or infinite-lattice-summation approaches) map distinct crystals to identical representations -- is only illustrated conceptually (Figure 2) and never empirically validated with a controlled synthetic experiment showing baselines actually fail on such constructed pairs while PRDNet succeeds; the evidence for the core contribution is entirely indirect (aggregate property MAE).

Missing an important, closely related baseline: potential/Ewald-summation-based models (e.g., PotNet) that are specifically designed to handle infinite periodic/long-range interactions are not compared against, despite being a natural and strong competitor for exactly the problem this paper targets.

The paper does not clearly engage with prior work that already claims representational completeness (e.g., eComFormer explicitly claims to be a 'complete' invariant encoder); the manuscript should explain concretely why such claims are insufficient rather than asserting a general limitation of 'local encodings.'

Because the learned form factor f*_i is computed from the already message-passed, environment-aware node embedding h_i^(L), the diffraction branch is not cleanly disentangled from the graph branch; the large performance drop in the 'NoDiff' ablation could partly reflect the removal of an entire extra learnable module/capacity rather than a genuinely novel physical signal. A fairer ablation (e.g., replacing the diffraction branch with a parameter-matched generic MLP/pooling branch) is missing.

No reported variance across multiple seeds/runs; several reported improvements over baselines are numerically small (e.g., shear/Young's modulus entries), making it hard to assess statistical significance.
Code is not currently released (promised only upon acceptance), limiting independent verification despite detailed hyperparameter documentation.
The Miller-index-count ablation (Figure 4) is limited to only two properties on a single dataset (MP), not extended to the other benchmarks or properties.

Minor clarity/writing issues: inconsistent naming ("Crystalfarmer" vs "Crystalframer"), some informal wording (e.g., "obversely"), and somewhat verbose/redundant preliminaries that could be tightened to make room for the missing empirical validation discussed above.

strengths: The core idea of augmenting graph-based crystal encoders with a reciprocal-space (diffraction) representation to capture long-range periodic correlations is conceptually interesting and physically motivated.

The paper provides fairly extensive experiments across three benchmark suites (Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, Matbench) and multiple property types (energetic, electronic, mechanical, classification).

Ablation studies (diffraction module, multi-head attention, residual connections, edge features, pseudo-particle vs. X-ray form factor, number of Miller indices) are included, giving some insight into the contribution of individual components.
A detailed worked example (CaF2 case study) and an explicit invariance derivation are provided in the appendix, which aids reproducibility of the math (though not the code, which is withheld).
weaknesses: The central claim that diffraction-based representation is 'physically guaranteed to be unique' is overstated: true uniqueness of the structure factor only holds over the continuous, infinite reciprocal space, but the method truncates to a finite set of Miller indices (Cmax=8, up to ~1000 indices chosen empirically in Fig. 4). No formal argument or bound is given for why this truncated set preserves the claimed uniqueness property, undermining the paper's main motivation.

The invariance proof in Section 4.3 is conflated: the text claims invariance to the continuous E(3) group (arbitrary rotations/reflections/translations) but the derivation (Eq. 18-19) only proves invariance under discrete crystallographic point-group operations G that map integer Miller indices to integer Miller indices. These are not the same group, and the paper does not clearly reconcile this distinction, making the invariance claim at least partially unsubstantiated as stated.

The 'pseudo-particle' form factor f_i* depends on node embeddings h_i^(L) produced by the same finite-cutoff-radius graph message passing that the paper explicitly criticizes as insufficient for capturing long-range interactions (Fig. 2, Section 2). This creates an internal inconsistency: the environment-sensitivity of the diffraction features inherits the same local-encoding limitation the method claims to solve.

ReGNet (Nie et al., 2025), which is the most directly comparable prior work using reciprocal-space modeling and is explicitly critiqued in Appendix A.2, is never included as an empirical baseline in any of the main result tables, despite being highly relevant; the comparison is purely theoretical/qualitative.

Baseline results (e.g., for Matformer, eComFormer, CGCNN) appear to be re-run under the authors' own training protocol rather than taken from original papers, and some baseline numbers look noticeably worse than widely reported literature values (e.g., eComFormer formation energy MAE of 0.033 in MP table is much worse than typically reported), raising concerns about fairness of comparison and possibly inflated relative gains for PRDNet.

No statistical significance testing, multiple random seeds, or variance/error bars are reported for any table, making it difficult to assess whether the reported improvements (often in the second or third decimal place) are statistically meaningful.

Computational overhead of the diffraction module (summation over N atoms x N_hkl indices, and extra MLPs) is not analyzed or compared to baselines in terms of training/inference time or memory, despite this being an important practical consideration for scaling to large benchmarks.
Code is not released and is only promised upon acceptance, limiting independent verification of the implementation details and the non-trivial Miller-index selection and invariance claims.

The writing contains several inconsistencies and minor errors (e.g., inconsistent model naming 'Crystalfarmer' vs. 'Crystalframer', awkward phrasing such as 'obversely performance drop'), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The novelty relative to prior invariant/equivariant GNN architectures for CPP (e.g., eComFormer, eConformer, eqv2) and to ReGNet's reciprocal-space modeling is incremental; the main contribution appears to be replacing fixed X-ray form factors with learned ones and fusing with a standard graph attention backbone, which is a relatively modest architectural change given the strong claims made in the introduction.

strengths: Physically well-motivated idea: complementing local graph-based crystal encoders with a reciprocal-space (diffraction) representation that is naturally sensitive to long-range periodic correlations, addressing a real limitation of finite-receptive-field GNNs.

A formal invariance analysis is provided showing that the proposed structure-factor representation is invariant under crystallographic symmetry operations (rotation, reflection, translation, and space-group operations), which is a meaningful theoretical contribution beyond just empirical claims.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse, large-scale benchmarks (Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, Matbench) and comparison against a good set of modern baselines (CGCNN, SchNet, MEGNet, GATGNN, Matformer, Crystalformer, Crystalframer, eComFormer), with PRDNet achieving the best or near-best results in almost all tasks.
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the diffraction module, multi-head attention, residual connections, and edge features across all three datasets.

The learned pseudo-particle vs. tabulated X-ray form factor comparison is a nice targeted experiment that directly supports the core hypothesis that environment-aware scattering factors are more informative than fixed physical ones.

Good supplementary material: detailed hyperparameters for all baselines, a worked forward-propagation case study (CaF2), and an algorithm box, which aid reproducibility and understanding even without released code.
weaknesses: The claim that the diffraction-based representation is a 'guaranteed unique' / 'complete' real-space description is undercut by the practical truncation of Miller indices to a finite set H (controlled by C_max=8, ~300 reflections). This reintroduces a finite 'receptive field' in reciprocal space, which is conceptually similar to the local-encoding limitation the paper criticizes in prior GNN-based methods, and this tension is not adequately discussed.

No quantitative comparison with the closest related work, ReGNet (Nie et al., 2025), which also uses a reciprocal-space block; the comparison is limited to a qualitative critique in the appendix without reporting ReGNet's numbers on the same benchmarks, leaving the central novelty claim only partially substantiated.

Some ablation results appear unusually large and possibly indicative of an unfair/under-tuned baseline: e.g., removing the diffraction module (NoDiff) yields a bandgap MAE of 0.361 eV on MP, which is substantially worse than other pure graph-based baselines like Matformer (0.193) or eComFormer (0.153) reported in Table 1 using presumably similar graph-encoding ideas; this suggests the 'NoDiff' backbone may not be a well-optimized graph-only model, inflating the apparent benefit of the diffraction module.

Similarly, the X-ray form-factor variant in Table 4 underperforms even basic baselines without any diffraction module, which raises questions about whether the tabulated form factor integration was implemented/tuned fairly for comparison.

The motivating claim that 'distinct crystal structures are mapped to identical representations' by existing methods (Figure 2) is illustrated conceptually/visually but not quantitatively verified (e.g., by measuring representation collisions or near-duplicate failures on real datasets), weakening the practical significance argument.

No code release at submission time, and no explicit discussion of computational overhead (e.g., additional training/inference time or memory cost from computing structure factors over hundreds of reflections per crystal) relative to baselines, which is relevant given the added physics module.

No reported variance/multiple-run statistics for the main results tables, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (sometimes small) improvements over strong baselines (e.g., shear/Young's modulus gains on MP are marginal).
Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., 'Crystalfarmer' typo, dense notation in Eqs. 8–11 and the invariance derivation) that could be tightened for readability.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine limitation of local graph-based crystal representations (finite receptive field mapping distinct crystals to identical representations) and proposes a physically motivated remedy via reciprocal-space diffraction, which is a reasonable and underexplored direction.

The learned pseudo-particle form factor that depends on |Q|, local chemical environment G_theta(G), and atomic species is a sensible generalization over fixed tabulated X-ray/electron/neutron form factors used in prior reciprocal-space works (EwaldMP, PotNet, ReGNet), and the paper provides a clear conceptual critique of these baselines (Section 2, Appendix A.3).

A formal invariance argument (Eqs. 18-19) is provided showing that the constructed structure-factor representation is invariant under crystallographic symmetry operations acting on Miller indices and atomic coordinates, going beyond simple E(3) invariance claims made by many competing papers.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three major benchmark suites (Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, MatBench) and many property types (energetic, electronic, mechanical, classification) with consistent state-of-the-art or near-SOTA performance.

Thorough ablations: removing the diffraction module, single- vs multi-head attention, residual connections, edge features, number of Miller indices, and a direct pseudo-particle vs. tabulated X-ray form factor comparison, all of which support the claimed contributions.

A generality experiment (Table 4) plugging the diffraction module into multiple baseline architectures shows the module provides broad benefit beyond the proposed backbone, strengthening the claim that the diffraction/pseudo-particle idea itself (not just the specific architecture) is useful.

Good reproducibility support: open-source code claim, detailed hyperparameter settings for all baselines in the appendix, and a worked numerical case study (CaF2) illustrating the forward pass end-to-end.
weaknesses: PRDNet has substantially more parameters (20.9M) than most competing baselines (e.g., 0.2M-15.4M), and no parameter-matched or compute-matched ablation is provided; part of the performance gain could stem from increased model capacity rather than the proposed diffraction mechanism alone.

The invariance proof in Eqs. 18-19 asserts that the phase term (R_g h)·t_g is always an integer, ensuring invariance; this holds straightforwardly for symmorphic operations but is non-trivial for nonsymmorphic space-group operations (screw axes, glide planes) with fractional translations, which the paper explicitly sets aside as 'not directly relevant' without full justification—this is a potential gap in the completeness of the invariance guarantee for the general crystallographic symmetry group.

Computational/scalability cost of computing structure factors over up to ~300+ Miller indices per atom is not analyzed (runtime, memory, and scaling with system size/number of atoms), which is important for practical adoption, especially since the paper touts scalability as a motivation over DFT.

The 'Diffraction Module Assembling' experiment (Table 4) trains different baselines on heterogeneous, uncontrolled GPU hardware, which weakens the rigor of this comparison, even though acknowledged by the authors as a limited-time-window supplemental study.

The ReGNet/ReciNet baseline had to be reimplemented from scratch since the official code was unavailable, raising some risk that the comparison may not fully reflect the original method's true performance.

While the physics framing (structure factors, Miller indices, form factors) is extensive, the core architectural novelty is arguably a global Fourier-type positional/structural feature branch fused with a standard graph attention network; the degree of novelty relative to prior Ewald/Fourier-based long-range works, once the physics language is set aside, may be more incremental than the framing suggests.

No reported variance/uncertainty (e.g., multiple seeds, confidence intervals) across the numerous benchmark tables, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are statistically meaningful, particularly given many margins are small (e.g., MP band gap 0.151 vs 0.153 for eComFormer).

strengths: The core idea of fusing a learned 'pseudo-particle' reciprocal-space diffraction representation with graph-based real-space embeddings is a reasonable attempt to address the long-range interaction/non-uniqueness limitation of finite-receptive-field GNNs for crystal property prediction.

The paper provides a formal derivation showing that the proposed structure-factor construction is invariant under crystallographic point-group operations and E(3) transformations, which is a nice theoretical touch relative to prior Ewald/Fourier-based long-range methods that do not explicitly preserve this invariance.

Experiments span three large benchmark suites (Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, Matbench) and many properties (formation energy, band gap, bulk/shear/Young's modulus, metal/non-metal classification), with extensive ablations (diffraction module, multi-head attention, residual connections, edge features) and a pseudo-particle vs. tabulated X-ray form factor comparison.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: public code repository, detailed hyperparameter settings for all baselines, and a worked numerical case study (CaF2) illustrating the forward pass.
weaknesses: The claimed 'state-of-the-art across the board' narrative is undermined by the paper's own appendix tables: in Table 9 (JARVIS-DFT-3D-2021 using baseline numbers reported in original papers) PRDNet is worse than Crystalframer/ReGNet on band gap (OPT), band gap (MBJ), and Ehull; in Table 10 (MP-MEGNet) PRDNet is worse than Crystalframer and ReGNet on formation energy and band gap. This directly contradicts the main-text claim of consistent superiority and suggests the headline results in Tables 1-2 may partly reflect weaker baseline reproductions rather than a genuinely superior method.

PRDNet uses substantially more parameters (20.9M) than nearly all baselines (0.2M-15.4M), yet there is no parameter-matched comparison or efficiency analysis, making it unclear whether gains stem from the proposed diffraction mechanism or simply increased model capacity.

The key long-range baseline ReGNet/ReciNet could not be run with official code and was reimplemented by the authors with a modified hidden dimension to approximately match parameter count; given this is the most relevant comparator (also using reciprocal-space message passing), using an in-house reimplementation for the main comparison tables raises fairness/reproducibility concerns.

Table 4 ('Diffraction Module Assembling'), intended to show that adding the proposed diffraction module helps any backbone, instead lists several exceptions (GATGNN, Crystalformer, Matformer) where performance decreases, and the models were trained on heterogeneous, unmatched GPU hardware with no shared seeds/budgets, weakening the rigor of this ablation.

Several physical claims are overstated or glossed over, e.g., diffraction providing a 'lossless'/'guaranteed unique' representation ignores the well-known crystallographic phase problem and the fact that the proposed representation uses only a finite, truncated Miller-index set (Cmax=8, up to ~300 indices) rather than the full infinite reciprocal lattice, which could itself re-introduce aliasing/non-uniqueness that the paper claims to solve.

The number of Miller indices (300) is selected via a sweep on what appears to be the same evaluation data without a clearly separated validation protocol, raising concern about implicit tuning/leakage.

The writing is dense and over-engineered with many small/incremental architectural tricks (gated attention, triplicated query/key concatenation, etc.) whose individual necessity is not well isolated beyond generic ablations, and the contribution relative to prior invariant/equivariant transformers (Crystalformer, eComFormer) is incremental rather than conceptually novel once the mixed SOTA evidence is taken into account.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: existing real-space graph encoders can map distinct crystals to identical representations due to finite receptive fields, and the paper provides a convincing conceptual argument (Fig. 2) for why reciprocal-space/diffraction information can resolve this.

The core idea of a learned 'pseudo-particle' form factor that depends on atomic species, scattering vector magnitude, and a learned local-environment embedding is a reasonably novel extension beyond fixed tabulated X-ray/electron/neutron form factors, and is clearly differentiated from prior Ewald-summation/Fourier-based long-range models (EwaldMP, PotNet, ReGNet).

A symmetry-invariance argument is explicitly derived (Eqs. 18-19) showing the diffraction features are constructed to respect crystallographic operations, complementing the E(3)-invariance of the graph branch.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three major benchmark suites (Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, Matbench) and many property types (formation energy, band gap, elastic moduli, classification, exfoliation energy, dielectric), with consistent state-of-the-art or highly competitive results against a large and relevant set of baselines, including recent reciprocal-space methods.

Thorough ablation studies (diffraction module, attention heads, residual connections, edge features, number of Miller indices, pseudo-particle vs. X-ray form factor) that isolate the contribution of each design choice across multiple datasets, supporting the claimed importance of the diffraction module.

An additional experiment retrofitting the diffraction module onto several baseline architectures (Table 4) provides evidence that the proposed reciprocal-space fusion mechanism is broadly beneficial, not just specific to the proposed graph backbone.

A detailed worked example (Appendix C, CaF2) and algorithm box improve clarity and reproducibility, along with a stated commitment to open-source code and extensive hyperparameter documentation for all baselines.
weaknesses: Several formula presentations appear inconsistent or possibly erroneous (e.g., Eq. 9 and its restatement in Eq. 63 define q_ij as Q_i ⊕ Q_i ⊕ Q_i, i.e., three copies of the same query vector rather than involving Q_j or a distinct interaction term); if this is a typo it should be fixed, but if it is intentional the rationale is not explained, which hurts clarity and reproducibility.

The invariance proof (Eqs. 18-19) asserts that the phase φ(g,h) = (R_g h)·t_g is 'always an integer' for any crystallographic operation g, but this is not generally true for non-symmorphic space-group operations with fractional translations (e.g., glide planes, screw axes, or general fractional t_g), where the phase is instead a root of unity rather than exactly 1; the proof as written appears to implicitly assume symmorphic/lattice-only translations, leaving a gap in the claimed 'full' invariance to crystallographic symmetry.

PRDNet has a substantially larger parameter count (20.9M) than most baselines (0.2M-15.4M in Table 1), and while the ablation shows the diffraction module helps, no controlled comparison (e.g., matching parameter budgets) is provided to rule out that part of the improvement stems simply from additional model capacity rather than the proposed representation.

The claimed dependence of the learned form factor on the continuous scattering-vector magnitude |Q| (Eq. 5, Eq. 12) is in practice implemented as a fixed per-Miller-index output vector (Eq. 13, MLP_form: R^d -> R^{Nhkl}), i.e., a lookup over a finite, pre-selected index set H rather than an explicit continuous function of |Q|; this weakens the paper's emphasis on preserving 'full physical dependencies' relative to prior simplified methods.

No variance/uncertainty (e.g., multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is reported for the main results tables, making it hard to assess whether some of the (sometimes small) MAE improvements over strong baselines (e.g., PotNet, eComFormer, Crystalframer) are statistically meaningful.

The ReGNet/ReciNet baseline had to be reimplemented by the authors because official code was unavailable, introducing potential implementation bias into one of the most directly comparable prior methods.

The supplementary experiment retrofitting the diffraction module onto other baselines (Table 4) shows mixed results (several models get worse on some properties), which somewhat undercuts the narrative that the reciprocal-space fusion mechanism is universally beneficial, even though this is reported transparently.

Scalability of the approach to large unit cells (where both N atoms and N_hkl Miller indices contribute to a O(N·N_hkl) structure-factor computation) is not analyzed, and computational cost/runtime comparisons against baselines are absent from the main text.
